newsitem.title: BELARUS: Bankers alarmed by arrest of Belarus c.bank head.
newsitem.headline: Bankers alarmed by arrest of Belarus c.bank head.

text.p: Bankers and economists, alarmed at President Alexander Lukashenko's decision to sack and detain the head of Belarus' central bank, said on Wednesday her departure could prevent any hope of reforming a moribund economy.
Lukashenko sacked Tamara Vinnikova on Tuesday and she was immediately detained by police on allegations of corruption.
"Everyone knew Vinnikova would be sacked, but absolutely no one expected her to move from her central bank office to a jail cell, which is alarming," said a local banker who asked not to be named.
A Western economist, who also asked not to be named, said Vinnikova's sacking was a serious setback for economic reform in the former Soviet republic of 10 million people.
"It is a significant loss in terms of effective implementation of economic reforms and liberalisation," he said. "Reforms may slow further from almost non-existent."
The International Monetary Fund has already frozen most of a $300 million standby credit extended to Belarus and the World Bank has halted credits on concern about the pace of reform.
Privatisation has barely got off the ground and both the banks and the currency market face tight state controls. Lukashenko sees little need to bring in Western-style reforms.
Vinnikova, 46, had been an unquestioning supporter of Lukashenko when she was appointed, but she had shifted her position over time.
She opposed Lukashenko's decision to lower refinancing rates without consulting the central bank and the creation of a corridor to regulate the rate of the Belarussian rouble.
An official at the Belarussian prosecutors' office said on Wednesday that Vinnikova had been arrested. She was accused of "damage to the state of major proportions".
"This is an act threatening both president's foes and his supporters. It reminds one of (Soviet dictator Josef) Stalin's repressions of 1937," said the local banker.

He said Vinnikova, named head of the central bank in February 1996, was not one of the president's real opponents. "Lukashenko wants to show he can both pardon and execute, that this may happen both to his supporters and to his foes."
She previously headed the Belarus Bank, the largest bank in the country. Her deputy, Nikolai Korbut, will replace her as acting head of the central bank.
But Western and local bankers said they were not worried by the resignation of finance minister Pavel Dik. Lukashenko accepted the resignation on Tuesday.

"The minister was not a terribly highly influential person here. The resignation was quite expected,' said the Western economist, adding that acting minister Nikolai Rumas was unlikely to retain his post.
"It would be a surpirise if Rumas remained a minister for more than few weeks," he said.
Dik's resignation was the latest in a string of changes in Lukashenko's cabinet since the president won additional powers in a constitutional referendum in November.
